deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (from the previous page). The 'consecutive parts of the pentagon' (Consecutive Theile des Fünfecks) are those of Gauss's pentagramma mirificum, the self-polar right-angled spherical pentagon. The five parts are α=r=76°10'40'', β=90°−p=28°4'20'', γ=P=65°19'20'', δ=Q=62°31'40'', ε=90°−q=30°30'38''. Gauss has chosen them so that sin, cos and tan of every part are rational. The previous page also tabulates arg(a+bi) for the Gaussian primes above p=2,5,13,17,29,37,…: 45°, 26°33'54'', 33°41'24'', 14°2'10'', 21°48'5'', 9°27'44'', ….

PART 1: half-angle tangents and their decomposition.
- The page lists tan(α/2)=29/37, tan(β/2)=1/4, tan(γ/2)=25/39, tan(δ/2)=17/28, tan(ε/2)=3/11.
- Each is written as a signed sum of 'basic' fractions. A fraction k/l stands for arctan(k/l) = arg(l+ki). So the line encodes the factorisation of the Gaussian integer denominator+numerator·i into Gaussian primes. Reading the first term of α as −1/2:
  - α/2 = −arctan(1/2) + arctan(2/3) − arctan(1/4) + arctan(1), i.e. 37+29i = (1+i)(3+2i)(2−i)(4−i), with norm 2210 = 2·5·13·17 (the '2210' of the previous page).
  - β/2 = arctan(1/4), i.e. 4+i, with norm 17.
  - γ/2 = −arctan(2/5) + arctan(1/6) + arctan(1), i.e. 39+25i = (1+i)(6+i)(5−2i), with norm 2146 = 2·29·37.
  - δ/2 = arctan(2/5) + arctan(1/6), i.e. 28+17i = (5+2i)(6+i), with norm 1073 = 29·37.
  - ε/2 = arctan(1/2) + arctan(2/3) − arctan(1), i.e. 11+3i = (2+i)(3+2i)(1−i), with norm 130.

PART 2: 'Allgemeine Bedingungen' (general conditions).
- Gauss now lets the Greek letter denote tan of the half-part, so tan α = 2α/(1−α²), sin α = 2α/(1+α²), cos β = (1−β²)/(1+β²), sec δ = (1+δ²)/(1−δ²).
- The two displayed equations are then the Napier-type rules of the pentagramma, each 'u.s.w.' cyclically:
  (i) tan α · tan β = sec δ, i.e. cos δ = cot α cot β;
  (ii) sin α · sin γ = cos β.

PART 3: rational parametrisation.
- Put (1+α)/(1−α) = a/b, i.e. tan(45°+α/2). Then sin α = (a²−b²)/(a²+b²).
- Likewise put (1+γ)/(1−γ) = A/B, so sin γ = (A²−B²)/(A²+B²).
- Rule (ii) becomes (a²−b²)(A²−B²)/((a²+b²)(A²+B²)) = (1−β²)/(1+β²).
- Solving for β² (implicit step, mine): 1−P = 2(a²B²+b²A²)/D and 1+P = 2(a²A²+b²B²)/D. Hence β² = (a²B²+b²A²)/(a²A²+b²B²).
- For β to be rational, Gauss takes the case where numerator and denominator are themselves squares. Each is a sum of two squares, so he uses Pythagorean parametrisations:
  aB = 2tu·N, bA = (t²−u²)N, aA = 2TU·n, bB = (T²−U²)n.
- This gives β² = (t²+u²)²N² / ((T²+U²)²n²).
- Compatibility requires (aB)(bA) = (aA)(bB) = abAB. This gives 2tu(t²−u²)N² = 2TU(T²−U²)n², i.e. tu(t²−u²) : TU(T²−U²) = n² : N².
- In words: the areas of the two Pythagorean triangles (2tu, t²−u², t²+u²) and (2TU, T²−U², T²+U²) must be in the ratio of two squares. They must have the same square-free part, i.e. lie in the same 'congruent number' class.
- 'Woraus sich obige Vorschr. leicht ableiten lässt; oder aus d. Trigon.': the above prescription follows easily from this, or else from trigonometry.

RELATION TO THE NEXT PAGE. The next page treats the variants where numerator and denominator are 5-fold or 10-fold squares. The example on this page is not of the pure-square type. Here a/b = 33/4 and A/B = 32/7, giving a²B²+b²A² = 69745 = 5·13·29·37 and a²A²+b²B² = 16·69745, so β² = 1/16 is reached with a common non-square factor.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All five half-angle decompositions check numerically and as Gaussian-integer factorisations, provided the first term of α is −1/2 (the sign is hidden under an ink blot). Both pentagon relations hold for the numerical example, as does the algebra leading to β² and to the area-ratio condition.

Notation slip: Gauss overwrote a/b by t/u (and possibly A/B by T/U) in the 'Setzt man' lines. He then reuses t,u,T,U as fresh Pythagorean parameters, while the formulas continue to use a,b,A,B for the ratios (1+α)/(1−α) and (1+γ)/(1−γ). The derivation is consistent only if those ratios are read as a/b and A/B.

Gauss restricts to the case where numerator and denominator are both squares. This is sufficient but not necessary for β rational: only their ratio must be a square. He handles 5-fold and 10-fold squares on the next page. The worked example itself is of the non-square type, with common factor 5·13·29·37.

results.what: Rational pentagramma mirificum: five consecutive parts with all trig functions rational (tan of half-angles 29/37, 1/4, 25/39, 17/28, 3/11), with the half-angles decomposed via Gaussian-integer factorisation into arctans of Gaussian primes
results.modern_name: Rational (Pythagorean) realisation of the pentagramma mirificum; Gaussian-integer argument decomposition
results.usually_credited_to: Pentagramma mirificum: Gauss (notes published in Werke III); arctan/Gaussian-integer decompositions are classical (Gauss, Störmer-type identities)

results.what: Napier-type rules for the pentagram: tan α tan β = sec δ and sin α sin γ = cos β (cyclic)
results.modern_name: Gauss's pentagramma mirificum relations (Napier's rules for the right-angled spherical pentagon)

results.what: Reduction of rationality of β to β² = (a²B²+b²A²)/(a²A²+b²B²), and, via Pythagorean parametrisation, to tu(t²−u²) : TU(T²−U²) being a ratio of squares
results.modern_name: Pythagorean-triangle parametrisation; two right triangles with areas in the same square class (congruent-number / elliptic curve y²=x³−n²x condition)
results.usually_credited_to: Diophantus/Fermat/Euler/Frénicle for the area-of-Pythagorean-triangles problems; application to the pentagramma apparently Gauss's own

deep.surprise_reason: The pentagramma mirificum and its relations are well known as Gauss's. A systematic Diophantine search for fully rational pentagrams, reducing to Pythagorean triangles whose areas have the same square-free part (a congruent-number-type condition), is a notable unpublished detail. The tools are classical, however, so this is not a major priority result.

transcription_corrections: α line: the first term is −1/2, not +1/2; the sign is under an ink blot, and only −arctan(1/2)+arctan(2/3)−arctan(1/4)+π/4 equals arctan(29/37).
'Es sey tg ½ α = 𝔄 etc.': Gauss thereafter uses the plain Greek letters α, β, … for the half-angle tangents.

In 'Setzt man (1+α)/(1−α) = …' both t/u and a/b appear, one written over the other; the subsequent formulas require the ratio a/b. Likewise (1+γ)/(1−γ) = A/B, with T/U as an apparent alternative or overwriting.
The final remark reads roughly: 'tu·(tt−uu) : TU·(TT−UU) = nn:NN, wie Quadrat [zu Quadrat], woraus sich obige Vorschr[ift] leicht ableiten lässt; [besser als, struck] oder aus d. Trigon[ometrie]'.
